question: A 55-year-old man with prior smoking presents with acute dyspnea and wheeze. What is the differential distinguishing cardiac from pulmonary causes, and what drives disposition?

gold.discriminator: chest X-ray, ECG, and BNP/NT-proBNP to separate cardiac from pulmonary; consider D-dimer/CTA for PE
gold.threshold: hypoxia or respiratory distress -> supplemental oxygen and admission; pulmonary edema -> diuresis and afterload reduction, COPD exacerbation -> bronchodilators/steroids

answer:
**Framing.** In a 55-year-old man with a smoking history presenting with acute dyspnea and wheeze, heart failure, asthma, and COPD are syndromes whose signs (dyspnea, wheeze) overlap substantially, making bedside differentiation unreliable [1][28]. This is not a rare diagnostic trap: in ED patients with a known history of asthma/COPD (no prior HF) who presented with acute dyspnea, roughly one in five (20.9%) had new congestive heart failure as the final adjudicated diagnosis, and treating physicians recognized only a minority (36.8%) of these cases clinically [2][18]. This underscores why an objective, biomarker- and imaging-based work-up—rather than pattern-matching on wheeze alone—is central to the cardiac-vs-pulmonary differential in this population [1][28][29].

## Ranked differential

**COPD exacerbation** — most likely given the smoking history and the epidemiology of wheeze/dyspnea in smokers, though this presentation is exactly the phenotype in which HF is frequently missed [1][2][18]. Discriminator: BNP is characteristically low in pulmonary-diagnosis groups including COPD-type presentations (mean 61±10 pg/mL in a pulmonary-disease cohort; even patients with known CHF history but a *current* COPD exacerbation had low BNP, 47±23 pg/mL) [7][19][6]. Next test: BNP/NT-proBNP below the rule-out threshold (BNP <100 pg/mL, NT-proBNP <300 ng/L, or NT-proBNP <300 ng/mL per the COPD consensus) argues strongly against an acute cardiac driver and supports a primarily pulmonary exacerbation [4][8][13][16].

**Acute decompensated heart failure / "cardiac asthma"** — worth considering, and disproportionately underdiagnosed in exactly this population (prior obstructive lung disease, presenting with dyspnea/wheeze, no known HF history) [2][18]. Discriminators favoring this: markedly elevated BNP (mean 587±426 pg/mL in the CHF-with-obstructive-lung-disease subgroup vs 108.8±221.3 pg/mL without CHF) [3]; in a separate cohort, CHF patients had BNP 758.5±798 pg/mL vs 61±10 pg/mL in pulmonary disease, with an AUC of 0.96 for BNP separating cardiac from pulmonary disease [5][19][20]; and even patients with a pulmonary-disease history whose *current* dyspnea was due to CHF had high BNP (731±764 pg/mL) [7]. Next test: an elevated BNP/NT-proBNP above the rule-in threshold should prompt transthoracic echocardiography (ideally within 48 hours) to establish or exclude a structural cardiac abnormality [8][21].

**Asthma exacerbation / reactive airway disease** — worth considering; grouped with COPD in the same low-BNP pulmonary phenotype discussed above [1][6]. No further BNP-specific data beyond the COPD/asthma pooled findings were retrieved distinguishing asthma alone.

**Pneumonia or acute bronchitis** — worth considering; BNP in these groups is characteristically low (pneumonia 55±76 pg/mL; acute bronchitis 44±112 pg/mL), consistent with a non-cardiac driver [6].

**HFpEF (including occult cardiac amyloidosis)** — worth considering as an underlying substrate, particularly if the eventual work-up shows preserved ejection fraction; diagnosing HFpEF is specifically difficult in patients with COPD because exertional dyspnea can reflect either cardiac or non-cardiac comorbidity [29][30]. Cardiac amyloidosis is an under-recognized, potentially fatal cause of HF and has been reported at a prevalence of 6% among elderly HFpEF patients in one study, though this is a distinct research population (HFpEF cohort, not an undifferentiated ED dyspnea presentation) and diagnosis requires costly, multi-step investigation (monoclonal protein screening, cardiac biomarkers, cardiac imaging) [22][23][24][25][26]. This is not a first-line consideration in the acute presentation but may be relevant if HFpEF is confirmed and doesn't resolve as expected.

**Cardiac sarcoidosis** — less likely in this vignette as an initial cause of isolated dyspnea/wheeze; it is typically suspected when there is new-onset ventricular arrhythmia, AV block, or unexplained CHF [27], none of which are described here. Included for completeness given the cardiac differential, not because this case specifically suggests it.

**Arrhythmia-induced pulmonary congestion** — *(standard clinical reasoning — not from the retrieved evidence)*: an arrhythmia precipitating acute pulmonary congestion is a recognized mechanism of cardiogenic dyspnea, but no retrieved finding specifically addresses arrhythmia as a driver in this presentation; an ECG (recommended below) would be the relevant screening step.

**Acute coronary syndrome — can't-miss.** The guidance base for acute breathlessness explicitly draws on ESC guidelines for both acute/chronic heart failure and for non-ST-elevation ACS, indicating ACS is part of the differential requiring exclusion in acute dyspnea [12]. Next test: troponin — troponins (and CK-MB) have documented value in detecting acute myocardial infarction or myocardial injury [15].

**Pulmonary embolism — can't-miss.** PE is explicitly named as a "frequent CV event" to rule out in the COPD population, using age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs [10][14]. Notably, BNP itself is *not* reliably low in PE — in one series, BNP was higher in acute PE (207±272 pg/mL) than in the other pulmonary diagnoses, reflecting right heart strain, so a "high" BNP does not exclude PE and should not be over-anchored to a purely cardiac read [6]. Discriminators raising suspicion: ECG findings (tachycardia, right bundle branch block) or echo findings (RV dilation, McConnell sign) [11]. Next test: D-dimer using an age-adjusted cutoff (in patients ≥50, and a specific threshold in younger patients) to decide on CTPA; CTPA should be pursued when D-dimer is elevated or when dyspnea/clinical features are not fully explained by a COPD exacerbation [10][11][14].

**Anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction — can't-miss.** *(standard clinical reasoning — not from the retrieved evidence)*: no retrieved finding addresses anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction in this presentation; these remain standard can't-miss considerations to exclude by history/exam (stridor, angioedema, exposure) before or alongside the cardiopulmonary work-up.

**Tension pneumothorax — can't-miss.** *(standard clinical reasoning — not from the retrieved evidence)*: no retrieved finding addresses pneumothorax; this remains a standard immediate-exclusion diagnosis (unilateral absent breath sounds, hemodynamic compromise) requiring emergent clinical recognition, not biomarker work-up.

## Initial workup
Before any biomarker result is available, the immediate priority is clinical stabilization and exclusion of immediately life-threatening causes (tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis/airway obstruction) by history and exam — these are standard-of-care red-flag exclusions *(standard clinical reasoning — not from the retrieved evidence)*, since no retrieved finding covers them directly.

Once stabilized, the guideline- and evidence-supported first-line tests are:
- **ECG** — to screen for ischemia/arrhythmia and for findings (tachycardia, RBBB) that raise suspicion for PE; recommended when cardiac involvement is suspected in a respiratory patient [9][11].
- **Troponin (± CK-MB)** — to detect acute myocardial infarction or myocardial injury as a driver or contributor [15].
- **BNP or NT-proBNP** — the pivotal test separating cardiac from pulmonary etiology in this exact clinical scenario (history of obstructive lung disease presenting with dyspnea): sensitivity 93.1%, specificity 77.3%, NPV 97.7% at a BNP cutpoint of 100 pg/mL [4]; separately, BNP distinguished CHF from pulmonary disease overall with an AUC of 0.96 [5][20]. NICE and consensus thresholds converge: BNP <100 ng/L or NT-proBNP <300 ng/L (or <300 ng/mL per the COPD consensus) argues against acute HF; NT-proBNP rule-in thresholds are age-stratified (>900 ng/mL for ages 55–75) [8][10][13][16].
- **D-dimer (age-adjusted cutoff)** — to screen for PE, a can't-miss diagnosis that can itself elevate natriuretic peptides [10][6][14].
- **Chest imaging** — not directly detailed in the retrieved findings beyond its general role; the findings do not specify CXR performance characteristics, so its use here rests on standard clinical practice rather than a cited quote.

## What changes management
- **If BNP <100 pg/mL / NT-proBNP <300 ng/L (or <300 ng/mL)** → acute HF is largely ruled out (NPV 97.7% at this cutpoint) [4][8][16]; workup should focus on pulmonary causes (COPD/asthma/pneumonia/bronchitis), all of which showed low BNP in the cited cohorts [6][7][19].
- **If BNP/NT-proBNP is elevated above the rule-in threshold** (BNP ≥100 pg/mL acute cutoff per general guideline anchors, or age-specific NT-proBNP rule-in values of >450/>900/>1800 ng/mL depending on age band) → pursue transthoracic echocardiography (ideally within 48 hours) to establish or exclude a cardiac abnormality [8][10][13][21].
- **If troponin is elevated** → evaluate for acute myocardial infarction/myocardial injury as a contributor, per the ACS-inclusive differential in acute breathlessness guidance [12][15].
- **If D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cutoff, or dyspnea/clinical features are not fully explained by a presumed COPD exacerbation** → obtain CTPA to rule out pulmonary embolism [10][11][14]; do not let an elevated BNP alone override this pathway, since PE itself was associated with a higher BNP than other pulmonary diagnoses in the cited series [6].
- **If clinical suspicion for cardiac involvement exists in a patient with respiratory symptoms** (e.g., overlapping/ambiguous exam, disproportionate hypoxia, or exam findings not explained by airway disease) → obtain ECG and NT-proBNP as the recommended stepwise cardiac work-up [9].
- **Disposition** is not directly addressed by a specific admit/discharge threshold in the retrieved findings; what the evidence does support is that the *decision to escalate cardiac work-up* (echo, further cardiology-directed testing) is triggered by an elevated natriuretic peptide [4][8][21], and that a *failure to escalate* carries a documented real-world cost — physicians missed the majority (63.2%) of CHF cases in this exact phenotype [2] — implying that biomarker-driven reassessment, not gestalt, should anchor decisions about further inpatient cardiac work-up versus a primarily pulmonary management pathway.

## Evidence basis & uncertainty
The core diagnostic-performance data (BNP thresholds, sensitivity/specificity/NPV, AUC) come from observational ED cohort studies [2][3][4][5][6][7][18][19][20], which are lower-tier than a guideline but directly relevant to the diagnostic question. Guideline/consensus-tier support is present for natriuretic peptide thresholds and echocardiography timing (NICE) [8][21], for general natriuretic peptide cutoffs aligned with ESC/AHA guidance [13], and for the stepwise cardiac/PE work-up in COPD patients (Belgian multidisciplinary expert consensus) [9][10][11][14][15]. No guideline-tier source in the findings gives an explicit ICU-vs-floor-vs-discharge disposition algorithm for this presentation — that gap is real and should not be papered over; the "what changes management" thresholds above are anchored to test-ordering and escalation decisions, not to disposition levels of care. Missing patient information: vital signs, oxygen saturation, exam findings (rales, JVD, wheeze character, unilateral breath sounds), and prior echo/PE history would materially change the differential ranking above but are not given. Genuine clinical uncertainty: BNP/NT-proBNP has a "gray zone" between rule-out and rule-in thresholds not resolved by the cited findings for the intermediate range. Weak/absent evidence: no retrieved finding addresses anaphylaxis, upper airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, or arrhythmia specifically in this presentation, nor bedside ultrasound protocols, nor explicit ICU-admission criteria.
